## An excursion to San Francisco Monastery in Tlaxcala: sixteenth-century heritage

[San Francisco Monastery in Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/) is one of Mexico's early Franciscan architectural ensembles. The complex includes a former monastery and the Cathedral of the Assumption of Our Lady, offering an insight into how religious architecture developed in this region during the first decades after the Spanish conquest.

In 2021, Tlaxcala's Franciscan monastery and cathedral complex was added to the existing UNESCO World Heritage property “Earliest 16th-Century Monasteries on the Slopes of Popocatepetl.” UNESCO highlights the complex's historic architecture, freestanding bell tower and wooden ceiling in the Mudéjar style.

We include this monument on the [private “Shrines of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla” excursion](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/). Visiting the monastery is one stop on a larger itinerary; we do not promise that this separate excursion starts at the monastery itself.

## What to see in the monastery complex

Unlike the richly decorated Baroque churches of later colonial centuries, Tlaxcala's ensemble is distinguished by its early construction methods. Massive stone walls, open spaces and elements of the monastery layout adapted to local conditions have survived here.

The Cathedral of the Assumption of Our Lady is especially interesting. Inside, visitors can admire the wooden ceiling influenced by Mudéjar style, recalling architectural traditions from the Iberian Peninsula. The separate bell tower and surrounding courtyards set this complex apart from many later Mexican churches.

Explore this monument alongside the history of the city of [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/). The monastery represents an early phase of Christianity's spread through the region, while nearby shrines reveal how religious art and pilgrimage traditions developed in subsequent centuries.

## How the monastery fits the Ada Tours excursion

The [Tlaxcala–Ocotlán–Puebla pilgrimage](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/) starts with a visit to the [San Miguel del Milagro Shrine](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/), where Mass is scheduled. The group then continues to Tlaxcala and visits San Francisco Monastery.

Afterward, the excursion proceeds to the [Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) and then to [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/). In Puebla, the itinerary includes the [cathedral](/mexico/place/puebla-cathedral/) and the [Church of Santo Domingo with its Chapel of the Rosary](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/). The return journey ends in Mexico City.

This is a succession of visits to several historical religious centers of central Mexico. We introduce the monastery together with other shrines; the itinerary does not include a separate, several-hour excursion devoted only to its architecture.

| Stop | Main interest |
|---|---|
| San Miguel | Pilgrimage and Mass |
| San Francisco | Early monastery |
| Ocotlán | Baroque shrine |
| Puebla | Cathedral and chapel |

## Excursion arrangements: transport, guide and Mass

We offer a private excursion with an English-speaking guide. The pilgrimage includes private transportation, admission tickets for the named attractions and one Holy Mass along the route.

The exact time allocated to the monastery and opening hours of every church are not specified in this program. They depend on access to active religious sites, worship schedules and the day's overall arrangements. Some areas of the functioning monastery complex may be used for religious events, so local rules must be respected.

If architectural history is your main interest, mention in advance that you would like more time to explore the cathedral and surviving parts of the monastery. On a pilgrimage, the time is divided among several shrines rather than concentrated solely on the UNESCO monument.

## How Tlaxcala's monastery differs from Ocotlán

[San Francisco Monastery](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/) illustrates the relatively restrained early colonial architecture of the sixteenth century. The [Basilica of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) is known for its later Baroque decoration and a different tradition of devotion to Our Lady.

Visiting both monuments in one day reveals the contrast between architectural eras. Their religious significance also differs: one stop tells the region's early church history, while the other is associated with a mature tradition of pilgrimage and worship.

## Frequently asked questions about visiting San Francisco Monastery

### Is the monastery included in an Ada Tours excursion?

Yes. It is listed on the [route through the shrines of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/).

### Why is the monastery part of UNESCO World Heritage?

Tlaxcala's Franciscan monastery and cathedral complex was added in 2021 to the World Heritage property of early monasteries on the slopes of Popocatepetl. Its significance lies in its architecture and early colonial history.

### Are guiding and transportation included?

Our pilgrimage includes private transportation and an English-speaking guide. Entrance tickets for the named sites and one Mass are also specified.

### Can we spend the whole day at the monastery?

On the current excursion, the monastery visit is combined with other shrines in Tlaxcala and Puebla. A separate itinerary dedicated exclusively to the monastery is not described.

## Excursion to San Miguel del Milagro: the Archangel Michael's shrine in Tlaxcala

[San Miguel del Milagro](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/) is an active Catholic shrine in the Mexican state of Tlaxcala. It is associated with the religious tradition that the Archangel Michael appeared to Diego Lázaro in 1631 and showed him a spring that believers regard as holy.

The shrine's story should be understood as part of the local religious tradition: it explains the origin of the pilgrimage and the site's veneration, but is not documentary proof of supernatural events or the water's healing properties. The church is also interesting for its colonial architecture and art.

We include San Miguel del Milagro on the [private “Shrines of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla” excursion](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/). It is the first stop of the day, with a Mass scheduled.

## The history of the shrine and sacred spring

According to tradition, in 1631 the Archangel Michael appeared to Diego Lázaro, a local resident, and revealed the location of a spring. A chapel was eventually built to commemorate the event, followed by a larger church. Pilgrimage traditions grew around the shrine and continue today.

The architecture combines colonial religious buildings, church paintings and carved decorative elements. Visitors may be interested both in the main church and the small chapel associated with the spring. The name “del Milagro,” meaning “of the miracle,” reflects the local history of veneration.

For pilgrims, it matters that the site is an active place of worship, not merely a museum. Religious services take place here and believers come to pray. Respect for local customs and asking permission before taking photographs inside the church are appropriate.

## How the visit fits the Ada Tours route

According to the [published itinerary](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/), travelers depart in the morning toward Tlaxcala and make their first stop at San Miguel del Milagro. A Holy Mass is included. The route then proceeds to the city of [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/) and [San Francisco Monastery](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/).

The next stop is the [Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/), known for its Baroque decoration. The group then travels to [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/), visiting its [cathedral](/mexico/place/puebla-cathedral/) and the [Rosary Chapel at the Church of Santo Domingo](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/). The group returns to Mexico City in the evening.

Every stop has a different purpose. San Miguel del Milagro is primarily about pilgrimage and Mass; in Tlaxcala and Puebla, religious experiences are accompanied by the architecture of different periods in central Mexican history.

## Included services and pilgrimage preparation

We offer a private itinerary with an English-speaking guide and private transportation. Tickets to the listed attractions and one Holy Mass along the route are included. The exact Mass schedule and time spent at each shrine are not fixed in this description.

| Route segment | Experience |
|---|---|
| San Miguel del Milagro | Shrine and Mass |
| Tlaxcala | Early monastery |
| Ocotlán | Baroque basilica |
| Puebla | Cathedral and chapel |

If attending a particular form of Mass, in a particular language or with a particular celebrant is essential, arrange those details separately: the general inclusion of “one Mass” does not specify them. The same applies if you wish to spend longer than the standard stop near the spring.

Modest clothing and respectful behavior during services are appropriate at religious sites. Access to the spring chapel and other spaces may depend on events and should be checked for the date of the visit.

## Who will enjoy this trip?

The excursion suits travelers interested in Mexico's Christian heritage and places of pilgrimage. It combines active shrines with historic architecture, making it possible to explore both on one journey from the Mexico City area.

If early colonial architecture is your main interest, see the [San Francisco Monastery in Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/) page. For Baroque interiors, consider [Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) and the [Rosary Chapel in Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/). The complete [pilgrimage excursion](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/) follows these themes in sequence.

## Frequently asked questions about San Miguel del Milagro

### Is Mass included in the Ada Tours excursion?

Yes. The [Tlaxcala and Puebla pilgrimage program](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/) includes one Holy Mass along the route, and San Miguel del Milagro is the first stop.

### Can we visit the spring at the shrine?

The spring is associated with the history and veneration of the site. Actual access and visiting conditions should be checked against the shrine's current rules.

### Why is the shrine called “del Milagro”?

The name relates to the religious tradition of 1631, concerning an appearance of the Archangel Michael to Diego Lázaro and the discovery of a spring believed to be holy.

### Can we book an excursion just to this shrine?

In our catalog, San Miguel del Milagro forms part of the complete route through Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla. We do not list a separate standalone program limited to this shrine.

## Excursions to Santa Bárbara Cenotes from Mérida

[Santa Bárbara Cenotes](/mexico/place/santa-barbara-cenotes/) lie near Homún on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. On one outing you can visit several pools formed in limestone, including open-air pools, waters beneath high rock vaults and partly dark caves. When choosing an excursion, the number of cenotes visited, transportation between them and time available for swimming matter more than finding one supposedly “most beautiful” pool.

Our catalog includes the [“Magic of Santa Bárbara Cenotes” excursion](/mexico/santa-barbara-cenotes/santa-barbara-cenotes-tour/). This is an **eight-hour** trip from [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/), departing between **9:00 and 9:30 a.m.** It includes **three or four cenotes**, an introduction to Yucatán's natural environment and opportunities to swim.

## How the excursion day works

After traveling to the Homún area, the group begins visiting the natural pools in the complex. Travelers move between stops by bicycle or using traditional local transport called a *truc*. It adds to the experience: paths link the cenotes, while water access and lighting are different at each one.

Some cenotes resemble open pools surrounded by vegetation. Others are inside caves, where daylight enters through openings in the limestone roof. In enclosed spaces, steps may be wet and light levels lower than on the surface. Comfortable shoes with good grip and enough time to descend and leave the water calmly are sensible choices.

Distinguish **the total number of cenotes in the visitor complex** from **the number included in your excursion**. Public descriptions vary in the number and selection of pools; our tour includes three or four cenotes. Confirm the exact stops for your date rather than assuming that every pool is included.

## What is included and what costs extra

Our excursion includes shared transportation, cenote admission tickets and the specified equipment: life jackets and transport between pools. **Meals, tips and personal expenses are not included.** The tour is conducted in English and Spanish.

| Feature | Ada Tours excursion |
|---|---|
| Departure | From Mérida |
| Duration | 8 hours |
| Cenotes | 3–4 as scheduled |
| Transportation | Bicycle or local *truc* |
| Swimming | Included as an activity |
| Meals | Not included |

If you prefer less time in the water, you can focus more on the rock chambers and natural views. Discuss in advance whether particular stages can be completed without swimming if necessary; this is a personal adaptation, not a guaranteed feature of every group departure.

## Preparing for the visit: water, steps and belongings

Bring swimwear, a towel, dry clothes to change into and nonslip shoes. A splashproof bag is useful, and documents and electronics should be kept somewhere dry. Follow the site's rules on life jackets even if you are a strong swimmer.

Entry conditions vary among cave cenotes: access might be by ladder, steps or platform. Travelers with reduced mobility should check the accessibility of **the exact pools** included in their selected itinerary. Facilities at one cenote should not be assumed to exist at all the others.

## A separate day excursion or part of a longer trip

The excursion is well suited to a dedicated nature day while staying in Mérida. It is also included in two of our multi-day routes:

- [“Mexico Lindo,” 8 days](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/): Mexico City, archaeological sites and Yucatán, followed by the journey's conclusion on the Caribbean coast.
- [“Viva Mexico,” 12 days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/): Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán, where the cenotes complement a longer cultural itinerary.

The choice depends on whether you want to dedicate a trip mainly to the cenotes and Mérida surroundings or combine swimming with several regions of Mexico. Compare flights, accommodation and other services in the full itineraries: sharing the same excursion does not make the conditions of the multi-day tours identical.

## Frequently asked questions about Santa Bárbara Cenotes

### Can I visit to swim without going scuba diving?

Yes. Our excursion includes opportunities to swim and explore the cenotes. Scuba diving is not included.

### How many cenotes will we visit in one day?

Our excursion includes **three or four cenotes**. The exact stops depend on the agreed version of the program.

### Is lunch included in the excursion price?

No. Meals are paid for separately.

### Is the excursion suitable for someone who cannot swim well?

You can explore the natural chambers without spending a long time swimming, but the route does include visits to pools. A life jacket is provided; discuss in advance whether individual water activities may be skipped and how access can be managed safely.

## Santa Bárbara Cenotes: a day of underground pools in Yucatán

From [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/), you can travel to natural limestone pools on the Yucatán Peninsula. Ada Tours' **“Magic of Santa Bárbara Cenotes”** excursion visits a complex near **Homún**, renowned for its cave and open-air cenotes with clear water.

The excursion lasts **8 hours**, starting between **9:00 and 9:30 a.m.** You visit **three or four different cenotes**, with time for swimming and travel between them **by bicycle or local transport known as a *truc***. Life jackets and admission tickets are included.

The route combines natural beauty with an introduction to Yucatán's culture. One cenote can resemble an open-air pond, while another forms a pool inside a cave: their shapes reflect the limestone geology and the movement of underground water.

## Why Yucatán has so many cenotes

Cenotes form in karst rock as water gradually dissolves limestone, creating cavities, some of which open to the surface. That is why one place may contain an open-air pool while nearby water lies deep beneath a rocky ceiling.

For Maya peoples, cenotes held **practical and cultural significance**, providing access to freshwater and featuring in religious beliefs. The history of any particular cenote can differ from that of the peninsula as a whole; a special archaeological ritual should not be attributed to every pool without evidence.

At [Santa Bárbara](/mexico/place/santa-barbara-cenotes/), you can compare light, limestone formations, reflections and the spaces inside several different cenotes in a single day.

## Which cenotes are in the complex?

The complex's official site lists **Cascabel**, **Chaksikín**, **Xooch** and **Pool Cocom**. They differ in how open they are: some pools lie beneath rocky ceilings, while others receive more direct daylight. This makes them interesting to compare in a single visit.

| Cenote | Character |
|---|---|
| Cascabel | Cave cenote |
| Chaksikín | Semi-open |
| Xooch | Semi-open |
| Pool Cocom | Open-air |

**The exact selection of three or four cenotes** depends on the chosen package and the complex's current rules. Ada Tours specifies **three to four** visits, so all four should not be promised without checking the ticket. The Santa Bárbara site also offers packages for three cenotes.

Whether a pool is open or enclosed does not indicate how safe it is: depth, access and swimming conditions must be determined on site.

## Bicycle or *truc*: traveling between the pools

The Ada Tours offer allows a choice between **cycling** and local transport for moving between cenotes. The complex's own website also lists bicycles, a small bus and the Santa Bárbara Express excursion transport among the options.

For active travelers, cycling makes the movement itself part of the experience. If you would rather save your energy for swimming and getting down to the water, agree on another transport option beforehand. Actual transport availability depends on the package, path conditions and the complex's rules.

The words *truc* and “truck” do not mean that visitors will necessarily travel in the back of an ordinary freight vehicle. They refer here to local tourist transport used around the complex.

## Swimming and safety in the cenotes

Swimming is possible during the excursion, and **a life jacket is included**. The complex's operator explicitly states that wearing a jacket is **mandatory**. Strong swimmers must follow this rule too.

Take care on stone steps and wet surfaces. Light changes inside enclosed cenotes, and water depth is difficult to judge from above. Swim only where it is permitted, do not jump into unknown water and do not enter closed cave sections independently.

Quiet waters and natural rock formations are particularly sensitive to damage. Follow local rules on skincare products, do not touch stalactites and leave no litter.

## What is included in the eight-hour excursion?

Our excursion includes:

| Included | Extra |
|---|---|
| Shared transportation | Meals |
| Cenote admission tickets | Tips |
| Life jacket | Personal purchases |
| Bicycle or local transportation | Personal expenses |

The trip lasts **8 hours**, starts in the morning and provides guiding **in English and Spanish**. The price of the standalone excursion is agreed when booking. Confirm the exact cenotes, type of transport, meeting point and group arrangements when choosing a date.

Meals are **not included in the Ada Tours offer**, even if the complex itself has a restaurant. Cenote admission and restaurant orders are separate items.

## Combining Santa Bárbara with a Yucatán itinerary

This is a full day excursion from [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/), best planned without another intensive program in the evening. Even though distances between individual cenotes are relatively short, the day includes the journey to and from the city.

On a broader trip through [Mexico](/mexico/), the cenotes offer a nature-focused alternative to city and archaeological visits. The main experiences are the water, cave formations and movement between different cenotes. They are distinct from exploring Mérida or the ruins of ancient Maya cities.

## Frequently asked questions about Santa Bárbara Cenotes

### How many cenotes are included?

The Ada Tours program specifies **three or four cenotes**. The exact selection depends on the agreed package.

### Do I have to be a strong swimmer?

Life jackets are provided for swimming and are mandatory under the complex's rules. Non-swimmers and travelers with reduced mobility should check the access, supervision and depth of the selected pool beforehand.

### Can I choose a bicycle or another type of transport?

The program allows **a bicycle or local transport** between cenotes. Confirm the availability of your preferred option when booking.

### Is lunch included?

**No.** Meals are not listed among Ada Tours' included services; the complex's restaurant does not automatically become part of the excursion.

### Where are the cenotes?

The complex lies near **Homún** on the Yucatán Peninsula. The Ada Tours excursion departs from the **Mérida** area with shared transportation included.

## Tours featuring Santa Bárbara Cenotes: eight or twelve days in Mexico

[Santa Bárbara Cenotes](/mexico/place/santa-barbara-cenotes/) are natural pools in the Yucatán Peninsula's limestone, near the village of Homún. Some are outdoors, while others are hidden beneath the rocky ceilings of caves. Clear water, underground chambers and tropical plants make them a distinct nature experience on a journey through Mexico.

Ada Tours offers the standalone [“Magic of Santa Bárbara Cenotes” excursion](/mexico/santa-barbara-cenotes/santa-barbara-cenotes-tour/), which also forms part of different multi-day routes. The outing lasts about **8 hours**, including visits to **three or four cenotes** and a choice between a bicycle and a traditional horse-drawn cart for transport between stops.

| Tour | Cenote visit |
|---|---|
| [“Mexico Lindo,” 8 days](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/) | Day 7, while staying in Mérida |
| [“Viva Mexico,” 12 days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) | Day 11, after other regions |

Both itineraries pass through Yucatán, but the surrounding days differ. Choose according to what you would like to see before the cenotes and where you want to finish your journey.

## “Mexico Lindo”: eight days from Mexico City to the Caribbean coast

[“Mexico Lindo”](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/) combines Mexico City with [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/). The first four nights are in Mexico City and the next three in Mérida. In Yucatán, travelers explore archaeological sites and spend day seven at Santa Bárbara Cenotes. On day eight, the route continues via Chichén Itzá and Valladolid to the Caribbean coast.

This option is suitable for travelers who want varied experiences in a relatively short time: the capital's landmarks, Maya history, freshwater swimming and a final drive to the sea. There is an important condition, however: **accommodation on the Riviera Maya after day eight is not included in the tour**. Ending at the Caribbean coast therefore does not mean subsequent days of beach accommodation are prepaid.

The domestic flight from Mexico City to Mérida is not included in the tour price. Private and group transfers vary by day, while the cenotes excursion itself is conducted in a group. These differences matter when comparing prices and logistics.

## “Viva Mexico”: cenotes near the end of a twelve-day route

The [twelve-day “Viva Mexico” tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) includes Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán. The Santa Bárbara Cenotes excursion is on day eleven, when travelers are already staying around Mérida. Earlier parts of the itinerary feature [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/), archaeological sites and craft villages, including [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/).

The main advantage of this program is its broader geography and wider range of cultural stops. The cenotes end a long sequence of city and historical visits with a nature-focused day. Compared with the eight-day route, it is worth considering your tolerance for more transfers and changes of accommodation.

“Viva Mexico” includes accommodation with a standard breakfast, the specified shared excursions and transfers, admission tickets to named historic attractions and the services of a certified bilingual guide. Domestic and international air tickets are excluded. It would be inaccurate to promise several days of beach relaxation simply because the itinerary visits cenotes: these are freshwater pools on a separate excursion, not a seaside hotel stay.

## What cenotes are and why Yucatán has so many

Cenotes form in karst limestone landscapes. Rainwater filters through porous rock and, over time, creates underground cavities, passages and pools. When part of a cave roof collapses or an opening forms, the water becomes accessible from the surface. Cenotes therefore take many forms: open pools, small holes in the ground and spacious caves.

Natural wells had practical and religious significance to Maya civilization. Underground freshwater was particularly important in areas without many surface rivers. Yet not every cenote was necessarily a place of ritual: discussions of their history should distinguish their general role in Maya culture from documented archaeological finds in an individual pool.

During the excursion, travelers can see both open and enclosed pools. Their light and water color differ, although they share the same geological origin. It is a way to discover Yucatán beyond archaeological cities and beaches.

## Swimming and traveling between the cenotes

The itinerary includes swimming in cenotes where it is allowed, observing their limestone walls and moving between stops. Transport around the site may be by bicycle or a traditional horse-drawn cart, often known as a *truck* or *truc*. The final method of transport depends on the chosen excursion and the local conditions.

The excursion module lists shared transportation, entrance tickets, a life jacket and transport inside the complex by bicycle or cart. Meals, tips and personal expenses are excluded. The trip lasts about **8 hours**, departs at approximately **9:00–9:30 a.m.**, and guides speak **English and Spanish**.

Swimming rules are set by the operators of the particular cenotes. Follow staff instructions, wear the provided life jacket, use authorized paths and avoid substances that may pollute the water. Hold the handrail and take your time on wet stone stairs. Accessibility of caves and water depth vary.

## Which tour is best for a first visit to Yucatán?

These programs share an excursion module but have different purposes. **The eight-day “Mexico Lindo”** is better for those wanting Mexico City and key Yucatán sites without a long stay in Oaxaca. Ending on the Caribbean coast makes it possible to extend a beach holiday independently, but extra nights must be arranged separately.

**The twelve-day “Viva Mexico”** suits travelers also interested in Oaxaca's culture, archaeology and crafts. The cenotes are then a nature stop within a longer cultural and historical itinerary.

The standalone [Santa Bárbara Cenotes excursion](/mexico/santa-barbara-cenotes/santa-barbara-cenotes-tour/) explains what the individual day involves. Find other journeys in the [Mexico tour catalog](/mexico/tour/) and the [adventure travel section](/interests/adventure/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours featuring Santa Bárbara Cenotes

### On which days do the multi-day tours visit the cenotes?

On [“Mexico Lindo”](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/), the visit is scheduled for day seven. On [“Viva Mexico”](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/), it is day eleven.

### How many cenotes can we see during one excursion?

The standalone program includes three or four cenotes in one day. The precise selection depends on the agreed itinerary and site conditions.

### Do I need to know how to ride a bicycle?

The description allows a choice between a bicycle and a traditional horse-drawn cart. Confirm your preferred form of transport when booking; the visit should not automatically be treated as a cycling tour.

### Are the life jacket and entrance tickets included?

Yes. The standalone excursion's included services list admission tickets, a life jacket and transport around the site. Meals and personal expenses are charged separately.

### Can we stay on the Caribbean coast after the cenotes?

The eight-day “Mexico Lindo” itinerary ends with a transfer to the Riviera Maya, but accommodation there is not included. To extend your beach holiday, arrange accommodation and other services in advance.
